items.text: The theater and the design are the best of the show. It's beautiful and very appealing. But it doesn't work that well live. The storyline isn't that entertaining. I went to see it one time and the stage kept breaking down and that made it very hard to stay engaged even in the more impressive scenes. It's trying to be something like the other Cirque shows, but it just doesn't really get there. So for me, it's only worth seeing just for the theater and the design. Otherwise, I would spend the money on another show. And I agree with Misty. Some people can love Cirque shows and hate Le Reve. But that's a separate discussion.

38 bucks for a used mechanical board. I figure I got about 38 bucks worth, maybe a bit more. It's just not quiet. The space bar rattles bad. Every time my thumb hits it, hollow clatter, like nudging a tray of cutlery. During the day I tune it out, but after midnight I find myself typing around it. And the E key repeats sometimes. Once every few paragraphs. Rare enough to forget, frequent enough I reread everything before hitting send. So "meeting" comes out "meeeting."

I messaged the seller to ask what switches it used. Got tired of waiting. Bought it anyway. Answer came a week later, after it was already on my desk. Brown switches.

Why I'm keeping it is the comfort. Each key has a small bump partway down. Fingers know a press registered without slamming to the bottom. I can get through a long email and my wrists feel fine afterward. The flat laptop keys never managed that. I thought about sending it back. Return shipping would have eaten a real chunk of the 38, and I'd be back on the laptop. So it stays, rattle and all.

I saw a theatrical circus show in Vegas. Its a good show, but I'm docking a star. The story's kinda hard to follow, and some songs just don't fit the action, they feel sleepy. The cast though, they're amazing. The acrobats, the muscles, the stamina, especially the women, who are underwater for several minutes at a time, that's wild.

They put it in a circular theatre, so no bad seats, you see everything. The stage is round, there are three entrances that they really lean on for the big scene changes. The whole setup, the lighting, it's a very nice place.

Tickets aren't outrageously expensive if you compare them to O or Love. I wanted more fire, more spectacle, but that's not a big deal. For a show with some storytelling and music issues, it's very entertaining, and really gorgeous to look at. I'd recommend it.

I've spent the last 2 years mentoring 5 junior engineers. Everyone says remote work is the fix for everything, but I think that's overblown for jrs still learning to code. Juniors don't really need tickets or documentation or meetings. They need to be present in design conversations, they need to watch others debug, ask questions before hours of confusion set in. That's the kind of stuff that just happens organically in the office. Working remotely means they have to know when to cut in on a call, set it up, explain a problem they might not fully understand. And that's a tough skill to have when you haven't really had a chance to learn it yet. I've seen the feedback problems. Short code review comments read as the final word, and not as a learning opportunity. And it takes longer, kills some of the momentum. When jrs got in-person pairing, whiteboard sessions, and had easy access to seniors, they improved faster. I'm not against flexibility or pushing for offices. Remote can be great for self-driven devs. But for jrs, proximity is a booster for confidence, context and instincts. And if we send jrs off with just a laptop and a calendar, we're dragging their development which means less good technical leadership in the future.

It was 3:17 AM. The industrial mixer hummed its low steady drone, vibrating through the soles of Elias's boots. Flour dust hung in the air catching the harsh fluorescent light like suspended snow. The sourdough loaves rested on wooden boards, their crusts still pale and soft before the final bake. Elias wiped his hands on his apron, the fabric stiff with dried dough and sweat. He moved to the front counter to check the lock. Ritual born of paranoia rather than necessity.

There it sat. The History of Salt. Hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. It had appeared every Thursday for six weeks, always placed precisely on the glass display case beside the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp indicated it belonged here. The bakery was not a branch of the municipal system. Elias picked it up. The cover felt cold. He opened it, expecting blank pages or perhaps a forgotten bookmark. Instead, a folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, landing on the counter with a soft tap. He unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension. Elias stared at the words. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. He looked at his own hands, red-knuckled and dusted white. He closed the book and placed it back on the glass, aligning the spine perfectly with the edge. Then he turned off the overhead light above the display, leaving the book in shadow.

Apple needs to be here, but from my own experience they deserve it. My school only allowed Apple laptops for middle and high schoolers, costing about double the price of a PC. My laptop broke like once a month. Never dropped it yet replaced the hard drive 5 times in 4 years, reinstalled the OS over and over. One time I saw my friends Macbook pro catch fire while he was watching a movie. The smoke alarm went off and it was scary. Apple support would not diagnose it, it would backup the computer, wipe it and restore the files. The same with my first iPhone. It was so bad, it was malfunctioning all the time. But Apple has now seemingly released a new iPhone about every 2 months. But I'll say one positive point, qualified. iPads are still the best tablets right now, but Android tablets will catch up eventually.

I've been dragged to Vegas constantly since I was a kid, so I've seen a ton of shows before I was 21. That gives me a real baseline for these productions. The good news is the circular stage setup is genuinely smart. From almost any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in these big theater shows. If you stay at Wynn or Encore, there's a deal where tickets are $99 instead of $125 for hotel guests. That helps.

Some individual acts are impressive, and the performers are clearly strong as hell. Aerialists, acrobats, whatever. But a lot of the feats feel like stuff I've seen done just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows. The bigger problem is the story. It's unclear, weak, or practically nonexistent. I left not really knowing what the production was trying to say. Also, too much goes on at once. Too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many wow attempts. A more restrained show would hit harder.

Aside from a few cool stunts, the whole thing felt average. I wasn't blown away, and no one I was with seemed overwhelmed. A few friends did enjoy it. So if you've never seen it, check it out, especially with the Wynn or Encore deal. But I wouldn't see it again, or pay full price a second time. It tries to be that stereotypical huge flashy Vegas spectacle where more equals better. For me, more just meant messier.

Went to Zumiez recently to buy a skateboard, went back to get the rest of the gear. At first it felt good. Me, my friend, and his younger brother were chatting with a woman who was putting the board together. She said she's the manager, has been assembling boards every single day while employed there, and admitted that on her bad days she's been mean to customers and other people. Then it took like 90 minutes to assemble it even though I expected 15. She stripped two bolts, replaced them in a way that made me think maybe they'll sell those bolts to someone else. She finally got her brother and another employee, who she said is also a manager, to help finish it. No apology. Zumiez will not get our business again. Heart was crushed.

Got this mechanical keyboard second-hand for 38 dollars and it has been a chaos ride. Seller was awful. I asked what switches it had, they took a week to reply with one word. I ordered it as a gamble. The board itself is well loved. Space bar rattles like a loose Lego brick. The E key repeats. Gets typoed like "theee" instead of "the". I love typing on it. Tactile feedback is fantastic. Comfortable for long work emails. Briefly thought of returning it but for 38 dollars, shipping back a heavy slab of plastic is not worth it. So kept it. I've grown fond of its flaws. If you don't mind a little DIY tuning and the E doubling now and then, it's a budget win.

Beware Turkish Airlines. Booked Harbin to Beijing, then Beijing to Istanbul. Harbin flight delayed, I missed my connection, at the airport booth no one took responsibility, no help rebooking. I slept at the airport. Next morning I asked for a ticket, they said flights overbooked, days to Istanbul unless I paid for business. I needed Istanbul so accepted. I am furious and in disbelief.

You bring one broken household item for repair, please. On arrival, go to the registration desk and get a ticket. That number is your place in the queue, so hold onto it. Volunteer experts will see who comes in first, so get your stuff fixed and pick it up before the volunteers leave at 4pm. They don't keep anything overnight. Take your time, be patient. And not all devices can be repaired, but you still want to bring your item. Please follow these simple steps so things stay smooth for everyone today.

A float valve manages trough filling. It's just a float that opens and closes the valve. Water drops and float sinks and opens. Water rises and float rises and closes. Once you get the water to the set level, it shuts off. For overflow, two common reasons. One is that there's some debris or mineral buildup and the valve won't fully close. Another is that the float is set too high, so the valve doesn't close until after the water has already overflowed.

Went to this spot on Sunday night, arrived 7:20. We just had a 10:00 show at the same hotel, so we thought it'd be easy. Food is probably good but we never got to eat. Digital waitlist is completely useless. Told to come back to pay at 8:23. We did. Then we just stood there till 8:40, and staff casually said we probably won't be seated until 9:15. Party of two. Zero solutions. If the wait is that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

Hi, to everyone at Enron. It's a rough patch right now. With everything going on here at Enron and what's happening out there in the world, this holiday season doesn't really feel like a holiday. We spent a lot of time discussing the all-Enron party planned for Dec 8. The company had different opinions. Some people thought it was a chance for us to get together and celebrate. Other people felt it was not appropriate. I understand both views. But after everything that happened in the past month we have decided to cancel the party. It's just not prudent to spend company money on a celebration now. That's a risk I don't want to take. I'm sorry. You guys are working hard and deserve recognition and something to celebrate. We will find other and more appropriate ways to recognize your great contributions during the holiday season. Ken

So a siphon moves water from one container to another and it works on gravity and air pressure. To get it started you fill the tube with water, makes it one continuous column. Then gravity pulls the water down the long leg which is in the lower container. That downward pull makes the top of the siphon low pressure, and outside air pressure on the source container pushes more water up the short intake leg to fill that low pressure spot, keeps the flow going.

The opening needs to be lower than the surface of the water where its coming from. That's because the force that makes it move is the weight difference of water on either side. If the opening is up higher than the source, its got to lift water up but the pull down is not enough to pull water down to fill it.

And air breaking the tube kills the effect. If air gets in there it breaks the chain of water molecules. So it equalizes the pressure, which is the same as outside, and then the differential that drives the flow goes away and stops. You got to prime the tube again with liquid.

The sourdough was on its second rise when I found it. Again. Every Thursday, it's right on the flour bin, always a copy of The Count of Monte Cristo, with the Richmond Public Library stamp. No clue how they get past that squeaky screen door without me hearing them, but honestly at 3 AM my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine. Tonight though, there was a scrap of yellow legal paper poking out like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron leaving white smudges on the dark cloth, and pulled it out. Page 142, the note said in spiky frantic handwriting. Please. I think they're watching the drop box now. A cold draft swept through the kitchen smelling of wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked at the dark front windows, just saw my own tired reflection staring back. Didn't open the book. Instead I carefully tucked the note back between pages, slid the novel into a brown pastry bag, and folded the top down twice to seal it.

Bought this used mechanical keyboard for 38 dollars. I reckon it's about that value, maybe a bit more.

The flaws are real. The spacebar rattles, not a soft click, more like a tray of cutlery gets nudged. During the day I don't really notice it, but at night it sounds awful. The E key repeats sometimes. So meeting becomes meeeting. Once every few paragraphs. Not a lot but enough to keep me proofreading.

The seller was slow. I asked what switches it had before I bought it. The answer came back after a week. Brown switches it is.

Surprisingly though, it's really comfy. The keys are cushiony and I can write long emails and my wrists don't complain. My old laptop keyboard is just flat so this is better.

Thought about returning it but it wasn't worth the hassle. So it just stays on my desk, rattling and repeating, doing what it needs to do.

Three stars.

Hi all, I'm [Name], Tom's brother. I grew up in a bunk bed with him until he was 14. So I've watched Tom's life up close and personal. The snoring. The stupid fights over the top bunk. And there are signs right there in the early years that this would be a remarkably reliable guy.

I mean it's Tom who shows up to rescue you from your own damn stupidity. So when I forgot my passport, he drove six hours to bring it over. That's just what he does. He's loyal, generous, and will do anything no matter how far out of his way, for you. And now, Tom, I'm really pleased you found someone who loves you like we do. And unlike me, this person chose to live with you by their own choice.

I rate it 4 stars objectively, but for myself it's 2.5. This was my first Cirque du Soleil show. I always expected to see a lot of backflips and extreme acrobatics. But there was much less of that and substantially more interpretive dancing than I thought. The performers were genuinely impressive. It was just not my style. If you really love this kind of theatrical spectacle, you'll probably enjoy Le Reve. I wouldn't pay more than $100 for it, though. Fortunately I went on free tickets and I'm very glad I didn't pay.

Old attendance registers are good for reconstructing daily life. Things that don't get captured in official histories. They show who came and who didn't, how regular attendance was, sometimes why kids missed. From that historians can guess about seasonal work, sickness, bad weather, poor families having to work, family responsibilities, migration, local emergency stuff. Also the differences by gender, age, where they lived, social class. So it tells you how school fit into work and household routines and what a community expected. Over years you see changes in how people approach school and in public health. But they're just what the school bothered to record. They don't really say what the kids experienced. Absences can get misreported, be incomplete, or be shaped by what the teacher thought. That's why you need to compare them with other sources.

Mara got the library book every Thursday at 2:17 on the bakery’s back step. Always the same copy of A Field Guide to North American Moths. It had a ghost pale county library sticker on the spine, plus a bit of flour stuck into the cover, like it had been helping around there. She had returned it twice. The librarians were too polite. Then, on the third week, she just left it next to her rye starter and kept quiet about it.

Tonight rain was ticking on the alley door. Ovens were breathing. She was shaping croissants, working butter into dough with her palms, then the latch went, tiny, guilty click. No one there. Just the book, bone dry on the wet concrete.

She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. There was a paper slip folded once, tucked between the Luna Moth and Promethea pages. Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs.

Mara looked out at the alley, the dented milk crates, steam from the drains. For a second the city seemed huge, then it didn’t. She tore a corner off an order pad and wrote, Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then she put the note inside the book, placed it on the warm windowsill, and unlocked the back door.

In our class we folded cardboard bridges, short beam, arch-y, and triangular folds. Same cardboard, lengths and widths as close as we could get. Set them on two supports, add little weights bit by bit and see what happens, bend, tip over, or snap. All handmade, few trials, classroom conditions. So this isn't engineering data. The triangular folds held weight more steady than the others. In this activity, how you fold it really does change how stable the model bridge is.

The book was on the steel table near the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang. A Field Guide to Coastal Birds, with the Harbor Street branch stamp on the cover saying it was due in March. The mail slot in that door was nailed shut years ago, but the delivery hatch next to it, the one the flour man uses, never latched properly. She'd been checking for eleven Thursdays. Asked the day staff, scraped the hatch looking for scratches, once stayed past four with her coat on. Nothing. But the book showed up sometime between two and four, and she was always at the ovens with her back to the door. Tonight she found a grocery receipt from Pell's folded into the oystercatchers page. The ink was blotchy from someone pressing too hard. It said she kept meaning to return it to the library, but when she passes her door and gets that bread smell she puts it down instead, and she can stop if she wants. Whoever left it smelled of salt, Marguerite thought, because the pages did. She grabbed a pencil from her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt, telling her to bring it Thursday and that she'd have a roll. She tucked the receipt back in, put the book on the hatch ledge, and set a warm roll in a paper bag next to it.

Toronto now, so no more Hydro Ottawa, but it is worth warning people about how they do billing. I had an account for a year while renting downtown. Then I moved back home to do my MA, cancelled the account properly and paid everything off. So I thought it was done. Turns out they kept pulling money from my account at random times for over a year. I called over and over, even sent them screenshots of the withdrawals, and the people on the line kept saying the account was closed, no debits happening. This only came out when my parents and I compared our bills. My banking details had been mixed up with their bill number because I had said I was moving home. Parents didn't see it because they always got refunds for overpaying, so credits looked normal. After hours on the phone and dealing with a bunch of reps, a manager looked into it, confirmed the mistake, and fixed it. Weirdly, they first said no refund, just an apology. Never giving out bank info for auto-debit again. The way they toss around customers' bank details should worry everybody.

3:40 in the morning, second batch of rye was proofing, and Marisol saw it again, there by the flour bin near the back door. The plastic cover was cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday in a row. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, stamped Eastgate Branch, three weeks overdue. Every time she carried it to the drop box on the way home. Every Thursday it came back, like the building itself had borrowed it. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A folded index card fell out of the barn owls page. It read: You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog now, she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. Signed R. Marisol read it twice, oven timer counting down. Outside the fan hummed, pushing warm air into the dark. She turned the card over. With her grease pencil, the one she uses to mark trays, she wrote: Rye's out at 4:15. Then she tore a heel off yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, put the book on top, and left the back door propped open about an inch.

I flew Ryanair when I was a broke student. My ex lived in Sweden, and it was the cheapest way to get to Stockholm. The whole experience was awful. At the airport they took my £20 bottle of L'Occitane shower gel because it was over the liquid limit, even though it wasn't. They said to get it back I'd have to go to the pharmacy, buy a 100ml bottle, and come back. I did and they had no idea what I was talking about. £20 gone, completely livid. Then at the gate they charged me £5 extra because I had a bottle of water in my hand luggage, which I'd bought inside the airport. Ryanair stopped flying from Liverpool John Lennon to Stockholm Skavsta, so I fly Norwegian Air now. Their customer service is poor too, ironically, but the planes feel newer and less outdated than Ryanair's.

I know how that feels. I got absolutely hammered by the rain Tuesday, and by Thursday half my Brandywines had split. You can see the seam running right down the side of the fruit. It's the classic pattern, dry spell then a deluge. The inside of the fruit takes in water faster than the skin can stretch. The Sungolds are mostly holding out, but I have a few of those looking like they might follow suit.

You can't really avoid the weather once it happens. The only thing that helps a bit is keeping that two day schedule you've got on a more even footing. But once the sky decides to let it all out at once, it doesn't matter much. You'll probably get a fair crop from the rest of the vines. Just pick the split ones off and put them to some other use.

It's a real headache with the Brandywines. That thick skin they have is a liability in a storm like this. You might get better luck with the Sungolds if you can keep them from getting quite so much water in a single go.

The College Board is a joke. A friend took the SAT subject test and the proctor just gave the room twenty extra minutes. Because she cares about integrity, and knew that advantage would mess up the test's standardized nature, she called the hotline to save future tests. The result is just brutal. After a quick investigation, they said they couldn't hold the proctor or other students responsible. But they somehow did hold my friend responsible. They found it in the evidence and just threw her scores out. They punish the honest one who is doing the right thing. And it's just unfair. They have no idea.

Most days, the book shows up Thursday. It doesn't come to the counter, it's wedged behind the flour bins by the back door, which means whoever leaves it knows I won't trip over it. It's always the same book, A Field Guide to North American Moths. Elmwood Branch copy, due date so far back the ink has gone violet. I've never seen anyone drop it off. By two o'clock I'm elbow-deep in rye dough, and at that hour I wouldn't notice a marching band.

The first few weeks I just left it on the shelf by the register. By Friday morning it was gone. Thursday, back again. Fine. People are strange. I'm a guy who talks to his sourdough starter, so I'm not judging.

Tonight there's a note tucked at page 114, the luna moths. It says, "They only live a week. They don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before it's gone?" No signature. Just pencil, pressed hard. I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling. Wrapped it in brown paper and set it behind the flour bins.

A room feels stuffy even if its temperature is comfortable. Humidity is a big part of it, high humidity makes it feel heavy and stale. Also if there's low air flow, the carbon dioxide and heat and smells just stay near the people. No air movement, so it feels closed and oppressive. AC can cool the air but it doesn't necessarily lower humidity or improve circulation. Opening a window, using a fan or the vent, all help air move, moisture goes down and it feels more fresh.

I've spent the last two years mentoring five junior engineers and I don't agree that remote is a win for everybody. What they need is not tickets or documentation or scheduled meetings. They need to be around a senior engineer and listen to design arguments. They need to watch somebody else figure out a nasty bug, see the process, and get answers before their uncertainty grows. You get all that for free in an office. At home, they have to figure out when to interrupt, set up a call, and explain a problem they don't really understand yet. That's pretty steep for someone who hasn't been around it.

I've seen this setup screw up feedback. A short note in a code review reads like a final judgment. The lag in getting answers kills forward motion. My kids, meaning the people I worked with, moved ahead much more quickly when they could pair up in person, use a whiteboard, and actually reach out to a senior. This doesn't mean scrapping flexibility. It's fine for people who know what they're doing and can direct their own efforts. But for a beginner, it's being around people that gets them where they need to be. That's how they pick up confidence, context, judgment. If you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar, you're going to end up with weaker technical leadership down the road.

A rain gauge is pretty simple. It just catches rain through a known area opening and gives you the depth in millimetres or inches. Think of it as how high water would sit on flat ground if it couldnt drain, evaporate or soak away. Most gauges have a funnel with a big opening which feeds into a narrower measuring tube. Its a narrow tube that shows you even small amounts. But the scale on the tube is marked for the area ratio, so you can just read the depth off it and it will be the true amount. The main error is wind. Gusts blow the raindrops past the opening so you're going to undercount. Evaporation and splashing before you read the tube will also throw it off.

Picked this thing up used for 38 dollars. Honestly, not bad for the price. It came out of the box with a bit of dust between the keys and some shine on the caps. What I expected from a second hand board, nothing worse. The good bit is that its comfortable. I write long emails for work and my hands don't feel as cramped as they did with my flat office board. The switches feel steady, not heavy. The case doesn't slide around on my desk.
There are problems though. The spacebar rattles when I hit it. Loud enough that I notice it on quiet mornings. The E key repeats sometimes. If I type too fast I get words like neeed. Not all the time, but enough I proofread more carefully. I asked the seller what switches it had, and they answered a week later, after it had already arrived. Not great. But for 38 dollars I kept it. Sending it back felt like more trouble than it was worth.

If you're bringing something broken, limit yourself to one item, grab a ticket at the front table, and hold on to it till your thing comes back. The volunteers call numbers in order, so hang around because they may need a call from you on something. They might have to order parts or they may not be able to fix it. Collect your item before 4:30, that's when volunteers go, and they're not going to store it for you.

Friday around 4:30, I walked in and there was no line, which was nice. Two people ended up at $130 which felt pretty steep. Before I went I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward I learned it cost somewhat more than what I was expecting to pay at a steakhouse. I was disappointed that steak wasn't offered. At that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices were lamb, prime rib, chicken. Those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the legs. The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. For dessert there was gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any. I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long I'd probably reconsider.

Old attendance registers are really useful for historians. They give us data on how people went to school day to day. The patterns really line up with what you would expect. Winter weather kills attendance. Flu outbreaks do the same. And then you get big drops during harvest, because kids get pulled off school to work. What this shows is that education was trading off against needing income. If an entire group was always absent, you can infer there was some kind of inequality or cultural resistance to school. But you can't take the numbers at face value. School administrations would doctor the figures to meet funding requirements or avoid being scrutinized. The registers don't say why students were absent. It's the teacher or headmaster's word. So the number is not necessarily true. The logs are just a way to track how the community functioned. To figure out what was really going on in daily life and social structure, you have to cross-reference them with other historical sources.

My school let us use Apple laptops, and I know why. Apple computers cost about double the alternatives, and they broke almost every month. I never even dropped my laptop, but the hard drive died five times in four years. Repeatedly reinstalled the OS just to keep it going. My friend's MacBook Pro caught fire once while he was watching a movie and the smoke alarm went off. Apple support didn't diagnose anything. They just back it up, wipe it, and restore the files. Same story with iPhones. I had the original iPhone. It constantly malfunctioned. Apple releases a new iPhone every two months now. Only the camera is slightly better. I'll credit them for iPad, it's the best tablet out there, but Android will catch up eventually.

A float valve lets you connect the trough to a pressurized water line. There is a float, normally a plastic ball or block, riding the water surface. The float is hooked to a lever arm. When the cows drink and the level drops, the float goes down and the arm tilts, which pulls a plunger or washer off the valve seat. That's how water runs in. As it rises, the float goes up, the lever pushes the plunger back to the seat. It narrows the opening gradually and stops the flow at the level you set.

Overflow is common. It happens when the washer is worn or covered with debris, so it can't seal to the seat. Or the float has a hole in it, so it gets waterlogged and never rises high enough to close the valve.
